## Why this matters {#sec-hash-why}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A hash table is a machine for remembering *which things you have seen* and answering "have I seen this before?" in one glance, whatever the number of things. You put the question down as a **key** — a number, a pair, a whole row of a matrix — and the table answers instantly: present? how many times? at which index? Hashing is how $O(n^2)$ "compare every pair" problems quietly become $O(n)$ "look it up" problems, with no sorting and no clever window.
:::

Here is the interview-shaped argument. Someone hands you $n = 10^5$ numbers and asks whether any two sum to a target. The direct reading of the definition — try every pair — runs about five billion pair checks ($\binom{10^5}{2} \approx 5\cdot10^9$): far past the budget of @sec-cx-budget. Now change the question you actually ask. Instead of "is there a $j$ with $a_j = t - a_i$?" (a search through the array), keep everything you have seen in a **hash set** and ask "is the value $t - a_i$ in my set?" (a single lookup). Same answers, a hundred thousand lookups, one pass. The pairs did not stop existing; the hash table turned "search the array for a partner" into "look the partner up by its value", and a lookup by value costs about as much as reading one array cell.

The two chapters before this one gave you two of the three great array summarisers: one pass with running state (@sec-arr-scan) and a table of prefix sums (@sec-pref). The hash table is the third, and the only one that works when **the interesting key is not an index**. You have already used one without looking inside: counting subarrays by their sum in @sec-pref-hash kept prefix sums in a map. This chapter opens the box. "How many times has this exact value appeared?" "Which prefix remainder did I last see?" "Have I visited this board position before?" — the value, not the position, is what you are counting, and the value range may be $10^9$ or negative or a *tuple*. A frequency array (@sec-arr-p5) can only index a small non-negative range; a hash table indexes *anything you can hash*.

**Where hash tables live in real systems.** Almost everywhere. Every Python `dict` and `set` is one; every JSON document you parse lands in one. Databases answer `GROUP BY` and `COUNT(DISTINCT)` with hash tables, and a *hash join* — build a hash table on the small table's key, stream the big table against it — is one of the two ways real engines join tables at all. Redis and Memcached are effectively one big hash table keyed by strings. Web crawlers keep a "seen URLs" set to deduplicate the web. Compilers and interpreters *intern* identifiers so comparing two names is pointer equality. Git looks up every object by the hash of its content. Game engines and chess programs hash board positions (Zobrist hashing) to run repetition detection and caches. The approximations you meet at internet scale — Bloom filters for "probably seen this URL", HyperLogLog for "roughly how many distinct users" — are hash structures that gave up exactness for memory. Distributed engines such as Spark compute "count per key" over huge data by *hash-partitioning*: every record with the same key is sent to the same machine, which then counts locally — the grouping idea of @sec-hash-keys at cluster scale. This chapter is the interview half of that story. String fingerprints (rolling hashes) get their own treatment in the strings part of the book, and questions that need *sorted* keys — the nearest key, the $k$-th smallest — stay with `map` and trees (@sec-lang-cpp).

**How the chapter is built.** Part A is five lessons: the machine and its guarantees (A1), how contest setters attack it and how to armour yours (A2), and then the three question shapes you will meet again and again — complements (A3), keys (A4), and counting without a table at all (A5). Part B is five patterns with two fully solved, stress-tested problems each. The next chapter, @sec-tp, answers several of the same questions a different way: when the array is sorted, two pointers find a partner with no extra memory, and knowing which tool fits is half of many interview answers. @sec-sw then puts a hash map *inside* a moving window.

::: {#fig-hash-idea}

## Part A — Lessons

## A1. Hash sets and hash maps: expected O(1), collisions, and what to use instead {#sec-hash-sets}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
The table is an array of **buckets**. A **hash function** squashes each key into a small integer, and the bucket number is that integer modulo the number of buckets. Keys that land in the same bucket are **collisions**; they are stored together in a little chain, and a lookup walks only its own chain. If keys spread evenly — they do, under the assumption mathematicians call *uniform hashing* — every chain stays a constant length, and "have I seen this?" costs one hash, one array read, and a couple of comparisons. That is the entire magic, and it is why the guarantee says *expected*.
:::

Walk one lookup of `key` in a table with $m$ buckets that stores $n$ keys:

1. compute the hash code $h = \text{hash}(key)$ — a fixed cost per key (per character, for a string);
2. find the bucket $b = h \bmod m$ — one division, or one bit-mask when $m$ is a power of two;
3. walk the chain at `buckets[b]`, comparing each stored key with `key`.

Steps 1 and 2 cost the same every time. Step 3 is the only variable part, and @fig-hash-chaining shows why it is short.

::: {#fig-hash-chaining}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
ch_keys, ch_m = [10, 22, 31, 4, 15, 28, 17], 8
ch_b = [[] for _ in range(ch_m)]
for k in ch_keys:
    ch_b[k % ch_m].append(k)                 # bucket = key mod m (an int hashes to itself)
assert ch_b[4] == [4, 28] and ch_b[7] == [31, 15] and sum(map(len, ch_b)) == len(ch_keys)


def draw(ax, p):
    for b in range(ch_m):
        y = -b * 1.15
        V.box(ax, p, 0, y, 1.0, 0.9, str(b), color="indigo", round_=False, filled=bool(ch_b[b]))
        prev = 1.0
        for j, k in enumerate(ch_b[b]):
            x = 1.8 + j * 1.8
            V.arrow(ax, p, prev, y + 0.45, x, y + 0.45, color="muted")
            V.box(ax, p, x, y, 1.1, 0.9, str(k), color="amber" if len(ch_b[b]) > 1 else "green")
            prev = x + 1.1
    V.text(ax, p, 0.5, 1.4, "bucket", color="muted", size=10)
    V.text(ax, p, 3.6, 1.4, "chain (keys in that bucket)", color="muted", size=10)
    V.text(ax, p, 5.6, -4.15, "4 and 28 collide: both are 4 mod 8", color="amber", size=10, ha="left")
    V.text(ax, p, 5.6, -7.6, "31 and 15 collide: both are 7 mod 8", color="amber", size=10, ha="left")
V.show(draw)
```

Separate chaining with $m = 8$ buckets and seven integer keys. Each key goes to bucket `key mod 8`. A lookup for $28$ computes $28 \bmod 8 = 4$ and compares against at most the two keys of bucket $4$; it never looks at the other buckets.

:::

**Load factor and rehashing.** The expected chain length is $\alpha = n/m$, the **load factor**. A table keeps $\alpha$ bounded by growing: when $\alpha$ passes a threshold, it allocates a bucket array about twice as large and re-inserts every key (**rehashing**). C++'s `unordered_map` grows when $\alpha$ would exceed its `max_load_factor()`, which is $1.0$ by default; CPython's `dict` grows when it is about two-thirds full. One rehash copies the whole table, but the copies form a geometric series — the same argument as `push_back` in @sec-arr-vec and @sec-cx-amortized — so an insert costs **amortised** $O(1)$. Put together: a lookup or insert costs $O(1 + \alpha) = O(1)$ *expected*, where "expected" is over how the hash codes happen to spread, and the occasional rehash is paid for by the cheap inserts around it.

**Chaining versus open addressing.** There are two ways to store colliding keys. **Separate chaining** (@fig-hash-chaining, and libstdc++'s `unordered_map`) hangs a linked list off each bucket. **Open addressing** (CPython's `dict` and `set`, and most fast contest tables) stores every key directly in the bucket array; a key whose slot is taken *probes* further slots in a fixed sequence until it finds a free one, and a lookup follows the same sequence until it finds the key or an empty slot. Open addressing has no per-node allocations, so it is friendlier to the cache, but it must keep the table well below full, because probe sequences grow quickly as $\alpha$ approaches $1$. For someone *using* a hash table the two behave the same: expected $O(1)$, worst case $O(n)$.

To make this concrete, here is a whole chained hash set built from Python lists. Write one like it once; afterwards no hash table is a black box.

```{python}
#| label: arr-hash-a1-chained
class ChainedSet:
    """A hash set from scratch: m buckets, each bucket a list (its chain)."""

    def __init__(self, m=8):
        self.buckets = [[] for _ in range(m)]
        self.n = 0

    def _chain(self, key):
        return self.buckets[hash(key) % len(self.buckets)]

    def __contains__(self, key):
        return key in self._chain(key)          # walk ONE chain, not the whole table

    def add(self, key):
        chain = self._chain(key)
        if key in chain:
            return
        chain.append(key)
        self.n += 1
        if self.n > len(self.buckets):          # load factor above 1: double and rehash
            old = [k for c in self.buckets for k in c]
            self.buckets = [[] for _ in range(2 * len(self.buckets))]
            for k in old:
                self._chain(k).append(k)


for _ in range(300):                            # behaves exactly like set()
    ops = [random.randint(-30, 30) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 60))]
    mine, ref = ChainedSet(), set()
    for x in ops:
        mine.add(x)
        ref.add(x)
    assert mine.n == len(ref) and all((y in mine) == (y in ref) for y in range(-35, 36))

spread = ChainedSet()                           # ordinary keys: chains stay short
for x in random.sample(range(10**9), 5000):
    spread.add(x)
assert spread.n / len(spread.buckets) <= 1.0
assert max(map(len, spread.buckets)) <= 12      # the longest of thousands of chains

attack = ChainedSet()                           # keys that are all multiples of 2^20
for i in range(1000):
    attack.add(i * 2**20)                       # every bucket count here divides 2^20
assert max(map(len, attack.buckets)) == 1000    # ... so all 1000 keys share ONE chain
print("chained set OK")
```

The last experiment is the whole danger of hashing in one line. The table ends with $1024$ buckets, but every key is a multiple of $2^{20}$, so every key is $0 \bmod 1024$ and lands in bucket $0$: one chain of length $1000$, and each insert walked the entire chain before appending. CPython's real `dict` is not hurt by this particular pattern, because its probe sequence mixes in the high bits of the hash; the toy table above uses only the low bits. @sec-hash-anti shows the same attack against C++.

**What the standard containers promise.** C++ `unordered_map`/`unordered_set` and Python `dict`/`set` all give expected $O(1)$ lookup, insert and erase. The differences that matter in practice:

- **Iteration order.** Python's `dict` iterates in **insertion order**, a language guarantee since Python 3.7. Python's `set` and C++'s `unordered_*` iterate in an **unspecified** order, which can change after a rehash. Never print "the first key" of an unordered container and expect the same answer on another machine.
- **Changing a container while iterating it.** In Python, adding or removing a `dict` key during a `for` loop over it raises `RuntimeError`. In C++, an insert that triggers a rehash invalidates every iterator, and using one afterwards is undefined behaviour. Erase inside a loop with `it = m.erase(it)`.
- **Reading a missing key.** C++ `m[k]` *inserts* a default value when `k` is absent; Python `d[k]` raises `KeyError` (a `defaultdict` inserts, like C++). @sec-hash-complement comes back to this.

The guarantee's dark corner: **all keys can collide.** The worst case of one lookup is $\Theta(n)$, so a whole pass over a table can cost $\Theta(n^2)$ — and someone who *knows your hash function* can choose keys that force it, exactly as the multiples of $2^{20}$ did above. For integers, libstdc++'s `std::hash` is the identity and the bucket count is a prime taken from a fixed table, so keys chosen as multiples of that prime all share one bucket. This is not hypothetical: on Codeforces, solutions get **hacked** this way (@sec-hash-anti). Python is safer for strings, whose hashes are randomised per process (SipHash, PEP 456), but a Python `int` still hashes to (almost) itself.

**The four-way choice** you should be able to state on demand:

::: {#fig-hash-choose}

```{python}

        ["structure", "lookup", "key order", "use it when"],
        ["freq[v] array", "O(1) always", "by value", "keys small, >= 0"],
        ["unordered_map", "O(1) expected", "none", "any hashable keys"],

    V.grid(ax, p, cells, colors={(0, c): "indigo" for c in range(4)}, cell_w=1.6)
V.show(draw)
```
